name: LZO (lzo1x)
workload: In-memory compress and decompress of silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes), single thread, lzo1x 2.10 level -1 against zlib 1.3.2 level -1, via the lzbench 2.4 results table.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 README table: lzo1x 2.10 -1 compresses at 500 MB/s and decompresses at 561 MB/s (ratio 47.45%); zlib 1.3.2 -1 compresses at 89.0 MB/s and decompresses at 297 MB/s (ratio 36.45%). About 5.6x faster compression and 1.9x faster decompression (derived from page data), at an output about 30% larger. First-party doc/LZO.TXT (mirror): 'The C version of LZO1X-1 is about 4-5 times faster than the fastest zlib compression level' (Calgary Corpus, 256 KiB blocks, Pentium 133).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); lzbench v2.4 Makefile OPT_FLAGS_O3: -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing -ffast-math -O3 -DNDEBUG (a few codecs use the -O2 variant); run options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
stars_or_usage: 49 stars on the unofficial GitHub mirror; ships in many Linux distributions and in the Linux kernel's own LZO port; bundled in lzbench
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0-or-later (the author sells commercial licences), so copyleft; block format with no framing or checksum in the core API; compression ratio at -1 is about 30% worse than zlib -1; many algorithm variants (LZO1, 1A, 1B, 1C, 1F, 1X, 1Y, 1Z, 2A) and a minilzo subset for easy embedding; the doc says it is free of known bugs, but CVE-2014-4607 (integer overflow in the safe decompressor on 32-bit) was fixed in 2.07.
caveats: Tier A rests on the lzbench 2.4 README run (public Makefile, gcc 15.2.0, EPYC 9555P), where the codecs are built by lzbench itself. On the same table LZ4 1.10.0 (550 / 3832 MB/s at 47.60%) and Snappy 1.3.1 (457 / 976 MB/s) beat or match lzo1x -1 on decompression and zstd -1 beats it on ratio, so the win over zlib is historical, not over today's fast codecs. The first-party figure comes from prose in doc/LZO.TXT with a Pentium 133 table that has no zlib row. The canonical site http://www.oberhumer.com/opensource/lzo could not be opened (egress block), so repo, license and release data come from the unofficial nemequ/lzo mirror (last release commit 2.10, 2017-03-01); no newer release is bundled by lzbench either.
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-c and the oz123 list entry for LZO, then the nemequ/lzo mirror (doc/LZO.TXT, NEWS) and the lzbench README results table
